items.title: A Peaceful Detective Mystery to Watch
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Welcome back to The Daily’s Sunday culture edition, in which one Atlantic writer or editor reveals what’s keeping them entertained. Today’s special guest is Lily Meyer, a staff writer who has published stories about the wisdom of Holden Caulfield , why making America’s houses bigger may have been a mistake , and the Seinfeld theory of fiction . Lily recommends watching The Sheep Detectives for a heartwarming mystery, listening to any song by the Hold Steady, and reading Brother of the More Famous Jack , by Barbara Trapido, if you want a good cry and a laugh. — Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor A good recommendation I recently received: My friend Eliza Brooke—a freelance culture writer who often covers movies—told me to watch The Sheep Detectives , which I had assumed was for children, but I trust her. I was absolutely charmed by the film and, at the same time, quite moved by its exploration of how we think and talk about death. Also, it’s a whodunit, and I love whodunits. Hollywood, could we please have fewer sequels and prequels and remakes, and more peaceful detective stories? The upcoming arts event I’m most looking forward to: I can’t wait to see the Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock show opening at the Met this October. I love abstract expressionism, and ever since I read Mary Gabriel’s Ninth Street Women —an exceptional group biography of five abstract expressionist painters, including Krasner—I’ve been fascinated by the arc of her career, which included creating government-sponsored public art during the Depression, making mosaics in the Long Island house she and Pollock shared during their marriage (meanwhile, he got an entire barn as a studio), and the flowering of her own painting practice after his death. Of course I’m excited to see the Pollock paintings at the Met too, but I’m most eager to see the Krasners. An actor I would watch in anything: Greta Gerwig. I saw Frances Ha , the gorgeous, bittersweet ode to female friendship that she starred in and co-wrote, a few weeks after I graduated from college—that is, at a moment when I was heartbroken about no longer living with my closest female friends—and I imprinted on her like a baby duck. The best work of nonfiction I’ve recently read: Vivian Gornick’s The Romance of American Communism . Gornick, a “red-diaper baby” raised in the working-class Jewish Bronx, set out to interview former Communist Party USA members and militants about what their political activity meant to them, years after the party had lost most of its following. The result is a surprisingly beautiful and often wrenching reflection on belief, belonging, self-delusion, and sacrifice. An author I will read anything by: Too many to name, so instead, I’ll give you a translator. I try to read—and believe I have read—everything that Megan McDowell translates. Her taste is impeccable, her style is flawless, and she works with some of the greatest Latin American authors writing today: Mariana Enríquez, Samanta Schweblin, Alejandro Zambra, and many more. A quiet song that I love, and a loud song that I love: “It’s Gonna Be Easy,” by the Texas outlaw-country singer Doug Sahm, is a soft, melodic lament for a relationship the singer wishes would be easier to forget. (A recommendation to go with it: Callie Collins’s novel Walk Softly on This Heart of Mine , whose protagonist is loosely inspired by Sahm. Like the song, the book is a gentle heartbreaker.) A loud song is “Waiting Room,” by my D.C. hometown heroes Fugazi. My husband and I asked the DJ to play it at our wedding, and the resulting mini–mosh pit is one of my favorite memories of the night. A musical artist who means a lot to me: The Hold Steady. I’ve been going to their shows since I was 14, and seeing them live is the closest I’ve ever come to a religious experience. Hold Steady fans are real diehards, and the band’s lead singer, Craig Finn, believes fervently that—as he shouts at every single show—“we are all the Hold Steady.” He’s right: We are. Something I recently revisited: I’m revealing a lot about my high-school self here, but one of my absolute favorite novels as a teenager was Chang-rae Lee’s Aloft , whose hero, Jerry Battle, is a New Jersey dad hiding from his emotions about family and aging by flying private planes. I revisited it before reviewing Lee’s new novel, A Tender Age , and was relieved that I loved it even more than I did at 15. A favorite story I’ve read in The Atlantic : I’m not sure if “favorite” is the right word here, but Spencer Kornhaber’s essay about the singer Lizzo and her downward mobility has been haunting me since I read it. Spencer, I want you to know that introducing me to the concept of the Khia Asylum was not nice! Something delightful introduced to me by a kid in my life: My toddler recently became obsessed with the book Chirri & Chirra , written and illustrated by Kaya Doi and translated from Japanese by Yuki Kaneko. It is so delightful. Doi’s illustrations are lovely, and the heroines’ sweet little adventure through the forest is a dream day. At the end, Chirri and Chirra go to a forest concert, and my daughter loves to sing “La-la-la” along with me as I read—it’s the best. The last thing that made me cry: Brother of the More Famous Jack , by Barbara Trapido. It’s a sharp, generous tale of yearning and innocence, and its descriptions are my favorite kind, economical and precise. Its plot twist made me cry, but so did the intensity and joy of its narrator’s longing. The last thing that made me snort with laughter: Also Brother of the More Famous Jack . I’m telling you, you need to read this book. Here are three Sunday reads from The Atlantic : Americans are spending luxury dollars for dive-bar service. Logging in was never supposed to be this complicated. A reverse Ellis Island The Week Ahead Mayday , an action comedy about an American pilot stranded in Cold War Russia who teams up with a former KGB agent (out Friday on Apple TV) Season 2 of The Gentlemen , a crime-comedy series about an aristocrat and his partner expanding their criminal empire into Italy (streaming Thursday on Netflix) The Disappearers , a novel by Marlon James about a group of gay men whose lives are transformed after a mob attack in 1988 Kingston (out Tuesday) Essay 20th Century Fox / Getty We’re Living in the World Dolly Parton Built By Spencer Kornhaber Dolly Parton’s death at age 80 comes at a time when her influence seems at its peak. Country music is surging, female singer-songwriters are on top, and audiences seem hungry for honest idiosyncracy—for figures who, like Dolly, transmit their inner truth to mass audiences in a voice that’s clear yet scraggly. But Parton’s greatest legacy is existential in nature. Piling on wigs and feathers, she showed that you can be yourself while playing a character. Read the full article. items.title: My Weekend at Adult Summer Camp
items.description: A t Camp Social , where grown women return to girlhood, friendship has no preamble. Within 15 minutes of meeting eight of the campers from Cabin 3, I learned this: In their 50s and 60s, they have no use for the menstrual discs in the camp swag bag; one of them found online dating so depressing after her divorce that she’s given up entirely; when they laugh, they pee a little; they feel like they’ve known one another for years, even though most of them met last night. The campers signed up for this weekend-long adult summer camp for exactly this purpose—to make new friends. On August 21, more than 400 women, some as young as 21, some older than 80, arrived at what usually is a children’s sleepaway camp in the Poconos to spend the weekend bunking in twin beds in log cabins, climbing the ropes course, developing middle-school-level inside jokes, making friendship bracelets, and performing choreographed dances at the flagpole to Cher’s “Believe” and Shania Twain’s “Man! I Feel Like a Woman!” Everyone at Camp Social, regardless of age, is referred to as a “girl.” The camp promises to recreate a childhood experience so that grown-ups can bond with one another as easily as they might have as kids. I signed myself up because I wanted to know what kinds of adults would go back to summer camp and how seriously they would take it. Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic My new home for the weekend with more than 400 possible friends-to-be The girls of Cabin 3 were all in. When they were younger, they told me, making friends did feel more straightforward. But then they got jobs that kept them late at the office, or their kids grew up, or they stopped drinking, and the friendships they’d made with other parents or neighbors faded. They began wondering: How do you meet new people? Where do you go? None of these women ever really thought they’d end up at an adult summer camp, but they saw ads for it and thought, Maybe I’ll give that a try . Which is how they found themselves at breakfast in the mess hall, cross-talking at Gilmore Girls speed, comparing notes on their adult sons, laughing when one revealed her favorite prank—taking a picture of her cleavage on the disposable cameras passed out at weddings. Over the hollering, Jackie Prendergast, a retiree who smiles so wide she shows both rows of teeth, told me that Cabin 3 has decided that its mascot for the weekend would be the flamingo. When a flamingo loses essential nutrients, as it does when reproducing, the pigment begins to drain from its feathers. With time and nourishment, though, the pink returns. “We’ve lost our color, but we’re going to get it back,” Jackie said. Ten minutes later, we headed to archery. Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic The vibes were, indeed, good. T he night before , Camp Social’s girls had gathered in the barn for a dance where a band (all male, all handsome) played Prince, Michael Jackson, and Bruno Mars covers. Liv Schreiber, the camp’s 29-year-old founder, took the stage in her Camp Social shirt. “Welcome to camp!” she shouted, then launched into an ecstatic speech about the weekend ahead. If anyone’s job could be described as “friend maker,” it is Schreiber’s. She is the type of person who skips more than she walks, makes it a point to memorize campers’ names, and, as I witnessed when we met up in New York City before camp, can form a real connection with strangers in a coffee shop in 10 minutes flat. She was working in real estate when she launched a viral matchmaking Instagram account and a matchmaking-party business, which morphed into events for adults to meet new friends. She opened Camp Social in 2023 to relive her own sleepaway-camp experience and to give women a place to meet. The waitlist, she told me, now runs north of 60,000 people. Adult summer camps have been cropping over the past couple of decades—one even dates back to the 1970s—but many of them are co-ed and have the feel of either Club Med in the woods or an all-out bacchanalia. Schreiber’s is one of the only all-female options with an explicit friend-making focus. Bubble letters on the camp bulletin board read, You Haven’t Met All The People Who Are Going to Love You ; the camp’s tagline promises that “99% of campers arrive solo and 100% leave as friends.” To get the crowd riled up at that opening camp dance, Schreiber asked, with genuine enthusiasm, “Who wants to meet a new friend?” Hundreds of hands went up. Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic Mornings at the flagpole included choreographed dances to Cher’s “Believe” and Shania Twain’s “Man! I Feel Like a Woman!” That “99% arrive solo” isn’t technically true. Mother-daughter duos and friends arrive together, and returning campers offer wisdom such as: Get to the Soffe-shorts distribution early to get your size, do not miss the Saturday pool party, and be sure to lean back right before the water slide spits you out into the lake. Even so, Schreiber has designed the camp for people to make new connections. Before arrival, campers received a guide titled “How to Camp Social,” which encouraged them to reconnect with their childhood self—the person “who made a friend at the playground in four minutes flat, who didn’t ask if she was too much or not enough.” The camp’s “10-Foot Rule” says that if you’re within 10 feet of another camper, you should smile and say hi. Bunks are grouped by age, but other than that, women are encouraged to make friends outside their generation. The counselors (all female) are trained to be welcoming, Schreiber said. They dance with campers at mealtimes, cheer when someone reaches (or tries to reach) the top of the rock wall, and shout out “Camp Social?!”—a cue for campers to circle their hips and respond with a Kool-Aid-Man-style “Ohhhhh yeaaaahhhh.” Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic The girls of Cabin 3 Who needs this kind of help making friends as an adult? Before I arrived, I’d wondered how many socially anxious people I might meet. Maybe the shyer campers were making themselves scarce, like Cabin 3’s mysterious tenth bunkmate, who kept to herself, or the girl in my cabin who disappeared when we all got ready for Saturday night’s camp disco. But most of the women there seemed capable enough of making friends; they were just in a moment in their life when opportunities to find those relationships felt scarcer. Compared with men, whose friendship skills are more often lamented, women do typically have more friends and are less likely to be severely socially isolated. But having a lot of friends doesn’t necessarily mean that a person’s social needs are getting met, and overall, rates of loneliness between the genders are roughly the same. The women at Camp Social were new mothers, grandmothers, empty nesters, divorcees, widows, and retirees; pretty much everyone was going through some kind of potentially isolating life transition. The average camper that weekend was 39-years-old, an age when many people are taking care of kids and aging parents, which doesn’t leave much time for friendship. For some attendees, camp simply functioned as a three-day lake vacation they didn’t have to plan—where they could do yoga on a paddleboard, attend an outdoor screening of The Princess Diaries , and drink signature camp cocktails. Last year, Schreiber told me, one woman in her 80s did nothing but archery the entire weekend. But many of the women I met came in order to feel like girls again, maybe with the hope that that would make friendship feel as easy as it did when they were kids. F or Cabin 3, Camp Social seemed to work a spell of quick intimacy. Of the cabin’s 10 girls, eight of them moved as a pack. (The ninth had come with her daughters and was spending time with them; the tenth I could never track down.) On the way to archery—along the lake and past the cabins, the pickleball courts, the pool, and the ropes course—the girls speculated about how someone would even use those menstrual discs, and Sandi Sullivan, who works for a construction company in Chicago, considered transforming her camp-branded bandana into a halter top for the camp disco, like the one her mom made her in the ’70s. When the archery instructor approached the group, he asked Vicki Petroski, a recent retiree, if she’d be a five—as in the fifth person on the range. “No, I’m a 10,” she replied. The girls cackled. The instructor blushed, and they cackled even louder. (Unlike the counselors, the camp’s staff members—who run the archery range, lifeguard the pool, and referee the camp Olympics—all seemed to be handsome 20-something men with British, New Zealand, or Australian accents.) Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic Jackie Prendergast, a flamingo regaining her color “In my 20s and 30s, I never would have talked so openly with other women I’d just met,” Jackie told me. It helped that Cabin 3 had all reached the age where, as Linda Gryn, a business-owner from Pennsylvania, said, “We no longer give a shit.” Some of the girls rarely speak about sex with their friends back home, but here, thanks to Vicki, whose daughter is a sex therapist, somehow every conversation seemed to come back to it. The group was too busy for awkward pauses, anyway. The girls danced: Linda, who had been a majorette in high school and dated a football player, watched the dance instructor like a hawk during morning flagpole routines. They painted (okay, while drinking mimosas) at the paint-and-sip. Vicki went tubing for the first time in about 30 years. “ Everything I did was 30 or 40 years ago,” she said. “When I turned 60, I said, Fuck it, I’m having fun again .” Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic Vicki Petroski and I survived tubing. But being 60 is not always as fun as being 10. At the afternoon pool party, as girls from Cabin 3 and I waved at Vicki, in line for the water slide, Christine—the most reserved in the group, a sensible lawyer with a sensible black bob—came over to me. (She is perhaps so sensible that she asked me not to use her last name.) Going to an adult summer camp at all, let alone by herself, was not usually her speed, she said, and she already has a close group of friends. But recently, the man she’d been with for 40 years “decided he didn’t want to be married to me anymore.” One night, he said “I love you” before bed as usual, and then the next day, he told her, “We’ve had a good run, but I’m ready for the next chapter of my life.” A good run? Christine remembered thinking. I thought that I was happily married . Her adult sons were trying to stay neutral; she was trying to be okay with that. Just then, Vicki went down the slide. The red-and-yellow half tube shot her multiple feet in the air, and we cheered when she emerged from the lake, grinning. Her curls were matted; the purple face paint she put on for camp Olympics was running down her cheeks. Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic The water slide was a hit among campers. Somehow, as the evening set in, everyone still had the energy for karaoke and the disco. The girls in my own cabin, all in their 20s, were getting along well, but if Cabin 3 had reached the peak of camp friendship, my cabin was still in the “friendly roommates who ask about one another’s day” stage. As we got ready to go back out, one bunkmate did my makeup; another, who had been to Camp Social three times, told me the “vibes were off” at the pool party this year because it was overcast. At karaoke, while other bunks performed as a group, we bobbed our heads and drank our alcoholic “Bug Juice,” garnished with gummy worms. Meanwhile, Cabin 3 was on fire. Sandi, whose camp-branded bandana she wore tied up as a headband after all, raged to Smash Mouth’s “All Star.” At the disco, they danced in sequins and jumpsuits to the songs that had been on the charts when Linda was in high school. Then it was Sunday morning and time to go back to real life. Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic “Y.M.C.A.” at the disco B efore the last morning flagpole , campers swapped Instagram handles and phone numbers. People seemed to have made friends, although a couple of younger girls I spoke with told me they definitely had not. They were ashamed that, even in an environment set up for friendship, they hadn’t connected with anybody. Those who had made friends wondered whether they would see them again soon or if they’d be only “camp friends.” When I asked my bunkmates whether they thought they’d stay in touch with anyone, one of them said rather ominously, “Only time will tell.” Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic Goodbye, Camp Social! But over breakfast, the girls of Cabin 3 helped one another download WhatsApp and started a group chat. Since then, they’ve been trading photos of the shirts they had tie-dyed and group pictures from the disco. One of the girls, Jacqui Moore, had painted a flamingo at the paint-and-sip, which has stuck as the group’s symbol. “Keep your pink coming!” Linda wrote in one message. Three girls who live close to one another in Pennsylvania are planning to get lunch. Others might join one bunkmate walking a marathon. (In accordance with their flamingo theme, they say their team name would be “The Flockstars.”) They probably won’t come back to Camp Social, though: The camp served its purpose. Maybe these women will get together annually to share the secrets they can’t with the people they see everyday. Maybe they’ll have a ball at Jacqui’s 60th birthday party. Maybe, like their other friendships, these will fade too. For now, they’re planning a reunion for next year. Greece—or maybe Moab?—could be nice.

items.title: Will the Real Dan Sullivan Please Stand Up?
items.description: W hat in the Dan Sullivan is going on in Alaska? Senator Daniel S. Sullivan is running for reelection. Daniel J. Sullivan is one of his challengers. And former Anchorage Mayor Daniel A. Sullivan recently endorsed the senator, while also declaring himself “the OG Dan Sullivan.” “It’s kind of hilarious,” Daniel K. Sullivan, a 33-year-old diesel mechanic and off-road fabricator from Wasilla, who is not running for Senate, told me. “I got a chuckle out of it,” Daniel P. Sullivan, a longtime teacher from Nome, who is also not on the ballot, told me. Control of the Senate could come down to a ranked-choice ballot that currently includes two Dan Sullivans (the Republican incumbent and the Republican challenger) and one Mary Peltola (a Democrat who was the state’s former at-large congresswoman). Republicans are worried that voters could be confused about which Dan Sullivan to select. Theories abound: Is this some sort of nefarious political plot by the Democrats? Or is it just that there are so many Dan Sullivans in the state that something like this was bound to happen? To get at the question, I reached out to half a dozen Dan Sullivans who appear to live in Alaska. I caught a second Daniel P. Sullivan, this one from Chugiak, while he was driving on a remote gravel road the other day. “The Dan Sullivan thing” has become a common topic of conversation, he told me, and his co-workers call him “the senator.” So many Dan Sullivans live in Alaska that his firearms purchases require a deeper background check. “So I don’t get mistaken for another Dan Sullivan,” he explained. (He said that he’s planning to move next summer so likely won’t vote for either of the Dan Sullivans: “Not really fair to vote when the outcome doesn’t affect me.”) Daniel F. Sullivan, a registered nurse, called me back from Palmer. “I often joke that I’m the real Dan Sullivan, and those are all imposters,” he told me. He said he grew up in New York with another Dan Sullivan in his high school, who was a better student than he was: “My parents would sometimes get honor-roll letters in the mail. I always wondered if his parents got all the bad letters about skipping school.” In Alaska, he found that his name had even greater benefits. A few years back, he had workers out to fix the electronic system in his hot tub, and the bill they promised to send never arrived. “I often wonder if the other Dan Sullivan got the bill,” he said. Whenever he’s part of a group going out to eat, the reservation is in his name in case it prompts VIP treatment. In this election, he said, he’ll probably vote but hasn’t settled on a candidate. “I won’t vote just because it’s a Dan Sullivan,” he said. This is not the first time a ballot has featured multiple Dan Sullivans. In 2014, Dan S. Sullivan was running for Senate for the first time when Dan A. Sullivan, the mayor of Anchorage, was running for lieutenant governor (the Senate bid was successful; the lieutenant-governor one was not). Then, in 2016, the former mayor briefly ran for the state’s other Senate seat. Had he won, both of the state’s U.S. senators would have been named Dan Sullivan. Neither of those Dan Sullivans returned my messages. T he Dan Sullivan who has put the name into the news is Dan J. Sullivan, who lives in Petersburg, a small fishing village on an island where Sitka black-tailed deer outnumber the roughly 3,000 people. His father was named Dan Sullivan. So was his grandfather. At the moment, so is one of his sitting senators. Shortly before the June 1 deadline, he filed paperwork declaring his candidacy. “We need a Sullivan who stands up for Alaska,” his website says. [ Read: Republicans have only themselves to blame for their Alaskan defeat ] The only Dan Sullivans he personally knows, he told me in an email, are in his own family: three Dan Sullivans and four more Dans who are not Sullivans. “We all have nicknames,” he said. “Mine will never be divulged.” He says that his campaign strategy mostly consists of maintaining his website and posting on social media. “Maybe some travel, but I don’t have much money,” he told me. (He has $8,400 cash on hand in his campaign account. The other Dan Sullivan has nearly $7.3 million.) His candidacy was immediately challenged by the National Republican Senatorial Committee, which referred to him as “Sham Candidate Sullivan,” and the Alaska Republican Party. Senator Dan Sullivan told reporters in Washington that it was “an insult” and that the challenger was “trying to trick my constituents to rig the election for Peltola.” “This is serious stuff,” he told CNN . “When people are going, Oh there’s two Dan Sullivans, isn’t that funny? No. It’s cheating.” The senator and his allies pointed to similarities between the challenger’s logo and the senator’s: Both are navy and mustard-yellow and feature at least one gold star. They accused the other Dan Sullivan of being part of a partisan plot engineered by a Democratic consultant. The Sullivan facing those questions told me the consultant had helped set up his campaign site and provided “tips on communications and basic campaign functions,” but said “she is not currently working for me.” They questioned his party affiliation. (He was previously a member of the Alaska Independence Party, but when that disbanded late last year, he switched his affiliation to the Republican Party, which he said was in line with his conservative views.) The director of the Alaska Division of Elections, which is overseen by the state’s Republican lieutenant governor, determined in June that the newcomer’s declaration as a candidate was invalid because it had been “filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.” The Sullivan in question appealed to the Alaska Superior Court. “I am running because I am tired of sitting back and watching our current Senator routinely fail to represent the interests of ordinary Alaskans like me,” he wrote in his defense. “The fact that Senator Sullivan shares my first and last names adds insult to injury, motivating me to raise my hand as an alternative choice for Alaskans.” Ultimately, the court determined that Dan Sullivan met all the requirements for making the ballot: It was his actual name; he did live in Alaska; he was over the age of 30. The whole experience, he told me, has been “daunting” because he feels unfairly singled out. “Typical of Sullivan to cry about it, make a nickname, and blame others,” he said, when asked about being called a “sham” candidate. Of the dozens of candidates running statewide in Alaska, he said, “only I have been accused of bad intentions (including one guy who is in jail). Seems unfair to me.” Both Dan Sullivans were on the ballot in the nonpartisan primary earlier this month, after which the top four candidates advanced to the general election. Peltola, the Democratic candidate, got the most votes, leading the incumbent Sullivan by seven percentage points. Daniel J. Sullivan came in a distant third with 2.5 percent of the vote, qualifying him for the general election—and showing that he could be a spoiler in November. His advancement angered Republicans, including the president. “The Crooked, Radical Left Dumocrats have put up another man named ‘Dan Sullivan,’ and they did this to take Votes away from our Great Senator of the same name,” Donald Trump wrote on social media. Senator Dan Sullivan’s early campaign ads have not mentioned the other Dan Sullivan, and when he talks in his speeches about an opponent, he references only Peltola. [ Read: Democrats’ great Alaskan hope ] But this is not the first time an election has featured similarly named candidates and accusations of political shenanigans. When John F. Kennedy ran for Congress in 1946 against a Boston city council member named Joe Russo, his allies helped recruit a janitor named Joe Russo to also run. In 2004, Representative José E. Serrano of New York was primaried by an unemployed former dockworker, Jose E. Serrano, who dropped out after being questioned about his legislative platform and not knowing what that was. In 2024, the governor’s race in Washington State featured Attorney General Bob Ferguson running against Robert Arthur Ferguson and Robert Benjamin Ferguson (the latter two Fergusons withdrew from the primary before ballots were printed). T he name Dan Sullivan is common enough. There was the offensive lineman for the Baltimore Colts in the 1960s. There was the race-car driver Danny Sullivan, who won the 1985 Indianapolis 500. There’s a theater and film director named Daniel J. Sullivan. Daniel was the ninth-most-common first name and Sullivan was the 107th-most-common last name in the United States in 2020, according to census records. There are nearly 5,300 Dan Sullivans in the country, according to the personal search aggregator Spokeo, and more than two dozen in Alaska. In Anchorage, there’s the Sullivan Arena (named for the city’s longtime mayor, George M. Sullivan, the father of the Dan Sullivan who was the most recent mayor of Anchorage) and Sullivan’s Steakhouse (named after John Sullivan, a 19th-century boxer). “Sullivan just seems to be the big thing,” Dan Sullivan the Wasilla mechanic told me. “But I don’t know any benefits from it that I’m aware of. I don’t get any discount at the steakhouse or anything.” The Dan Sullivan from Nome told me he would occasionally get random calls from people around the state confronting him about his campaign promises, especially when the Anchorage mayor and the U.S. senator were both Dan Sullivans. “I’d show my credit card, and they’d look at me and do a double take,” he said. “I got to meet all the Dan Sullivans. All the famous ones. I’m probably the least interesting out of all of them.” (He has since retired and has been traveling, and says he has not yet done his homework on which candidate he’ll support in the election). For the Dan Sullivans, it can be a little disorienting when the political ads are blanketing the airwaves. “It’ll say, Dan Sullivan’s ruining the Alaska fisheries! Or Dan Sullivan voted to raise your health insurance! I’m like, No, I didn’t! It wasn’t me ,” said Dan Sullivan the mechanic. “Or you’ll get an ad on the radio and it’s like, Dan Sullivan’s great for Alaska! Yeah, he is.” He’s not much into politics, so he says he’s unlikely to join the other Dan Sullivans in campaigning. He’s more conservative, so he plans to vote for the incumbent senator. As if things couldn’t get more confusing, there’s also a Dan Sullivan who has run for Congress in Massachusetts. There are so many Dan Sullivans that, at times, my attempts to reach the ones in Alaska went awry. I messaged a Dan Sullivan I thought for sure was from Palmer, Alaska, but instead located one in Cleveland, Ohio. He politely responded that his origins are in Brooklyn and Massachusetts. “I am Daniel M. Sullivan. My dad was Daniel P. Sullivan,” he said. Although he won’t be voting in Alaska, the intrigue has caught his eye: “I have been following this story with interest.” The Alaska race will be determined in November. At least in this election cycle, there’s room for only one Dan Sullivan in the Senate (and possibly none). But some other Dan Sullivans are getting ideas about future options. “Maybe one of us needs to run for president,” Dan Sullivan the mechanic told me. Or perhaps two? “You can pick anybody you want. As long as it’s Dan Sullivan.”

items.title: El Niño Has Become a Doom Loop
items.description: In the middle of the Pacific Ocean, along the equator, scientists have drawn a box. It’s a big box, two-thirds the size of China, yet hardly anyone lives inside it. This rectangular swath of open ocean is monitored by satellites and a network of moored buoys that measure minute changes in the temperature of the water, with an eye toward anomalies. Every few years or so, driven by changing winds and currents, the water temperature in this part of the ocean starts to rise; even a half degree Celsius above normal over months warrants a designation that an El Niño phase has begun. That’s enough warming to unleash floods and fires, drought and famine, around the world. The box is called Niño 3.4. Right now, it’s hot in the box. “Like a baby pool,” Kristina Tietjen, who spent most of August scuba diving in the middle of this mass of abnormally warm water, told me. Tietjen has been coming to the world’s largest atoll, Kiritimati, for more than a decade to study its coral reefs. She usually dives in a medium-weight wetsuit; this trip, her team needed only rash guards. It is still early in this El Niño cycle—which is likely to be the strongest ever recorded—but the waters around Kiritimati have already been 3 to 4 degrees Celsius above normal. Tietjen’s time on Kiritimati (pronounced like Christmas ) has allowed her to watch, in brutal detail, what these repeated warm-water cycles, playing out in a steadily warming ocean, mean for the great tropical coral reefs here, which were once near pristine. During her first El Niño, in 2015–16, 90 percent of Kiritimati’s coral reef died. Years of slow, partial recovery followed. This month, Tietjen and her colleagues, part of the Canadian scientist Julia Baum’s lab at the University of Victoria, discovered that nearly half of the island’s remaining corals had already bleached—a prelude, if warming persists, to death. When Tietjen comes back, she may well be swimming over a graveyard. Most of the world experiences El Niño’s ripple effects as the heat building up in the equatorial Pacific radiates into the atmosphere and around the globe. This means great gouts of rain in supercharged storms in some places; in other areas, crop-killing dry spells that can extend for months. Along the Pacific Coast of South America, torrential rains and landslides have forced the temporary closure of a main route to Machu Picchu, in Peru; deadly floods have swept through arid regions of northern Chile. Countries such as India and Ethiopia are enduring some of their driest summers on record. El Niños tend to mean more rainfall across the southern United States and drier stretches across a band in the North. Strong El Niños can mean record-breaking heat, and this one is shaping up to be unlike any catalogued in the past eight decades. A 2-degree-Celsius increase in the Niño 3.4 box typically earns the title of “Super El Niño”; we’re already past that threshold, and experts project that the warming could peak at roughly twice as high. “We are now pretty certain this will be an exceptional event,” Malte Stuecker, the director of the International Pacific Research Center at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, told me. Part of the reason Stuecker expects this warmth to keep building is that the buoys along the equator can detect water temperatures well below the surface. Down more than 100 meters, an enormous mass of warm water has built up and will rise to the surface in the months ahead. The amount of heat brewing in the ocean has produced one of those graphs in which the current year departs drastically from past trend lines, wriggling up erratically into unfamiliar territory. Although scientists continue to debate the extent to which climate change makes El Niño cycles more frequent or intense, they agree that these cycles are occurring in an ocean that is warmer than it was. Last Saturday, the daily global average sea-surface temperature reached 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 degrees Fahrenheit), its highest level on record , according to Europe’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. Even if El Niño cycles are not changing at all, as they spiral around that ascending baseline, the temperature peaks they hit keep getting higher, causing repeated blows to marine life and disrupting ecosystems in ways that may be irrevocable. Carlos Zavalaga, the director of the seabird lab at the Universidad Cientifica del Sur, in Lima, began to comprehend the magnitude of this year’s warming in mid-June, when he visited Macabi and Guanape Norte, two islands off the northern coast of Peru. He’d been hearing from colleagues about dead birds washing up by the hundreds on the coasts of Peru and Ecuador. He’s seen the news stories about flocks of hungry Peruvian pelicans swarming the fish markets in port cities looking for food. On the two islands, which just last year were thronged with pelicans, Inca terns, and Humboldt penguins, Zavalaga found empty nests, some with eggs and starving chicks. “They were abandoned islands,” he told me. These seabirds feed on schools of anchovies swept up in the Humboldt current, the cold, nutrient-rich upwelling waters that create bountiful fisheries off South America’s Pacific Coast. During El Niño years, that current gets displaced by warmer waters pushing east across the ocean, and these great schools of feeder fish can vanish from the coasts. The decline has been severe enough that Peru this month shut down an anchovy fishery that is a key economic engine for the country, with much of the year’s quota unfilled. Long before satellite monitoring, Peruvian fishermen noticed these cycles of warmer waters and dwindling fish stocks; they named the phenomenon, which peaked around Christmas, after the Christ child. References to El Niño in Peru’s scientific literature date back to the 19th century. In his three decades studying seabirds, Zavalaga has witnessed die-offs before. But it is the rapid-fire nature of these blows and the severity of the disruptions that make him so concerned. Just three years ago—the same year avian flu killed more than 500,000 seabirds—another El Niño slammed into the coast of Peru. The birds that had made a tenuous recovery since then now face the prospect of another die-off. “It’s like a boxing match: You have a first knockout, you try to recover quickly, and then you have a second knockout,” he said. “I cannot imagine what will be the scenario by the end of this year.” He doubted that the birds could go extinct, but some species might move farther south in search of colder waters. The coastline in Peru and the culture that depends on the fish and the birds could be permanently altered. When the warming started around Kiritimati, one of the few populated islands in the Niño 3.4 monitoring zone, Bill Newton, an island resident, was fascinated by how evident the changes were. He told me that the normally dry island turned sopping wet, and regular floods started washing out the roads. The wet brought swarms of mosquitoes (prior El Niños have led to outbreaks of dengue and chikungunya) but also clouds of dragonflies, which he hadn’t seen before. Higher-than-normal tides poured into seafront homes. Tuna, which can do well in warmer water, attracted dozens of fishing boats off the coast. Prevailing winds changed direction. Corals have a particularly hard time when water warms; they can’t move elsewhere, and they are sensitive to heat stress. As little as four weeks in water just a degree warmer than normal can cause bleaching, the loss of the symbiont algae that supply corals’ food and brilliant colors, according to Baum, whose lab Tietjen works at. Baum, an ecologist, has studied Kiritimati’s reef since 2009. After the El Niño a decade ago killed off nearly the entire reef, Baum began to consider the possibility that she would witness the obliteration of an ecosystem in her lifetime. In a 2018 paper in Science , she projected that successive bleaching events could occur frequently enough that coral reefs, which take roughly 10 to 30 years to recover from mass mortality, would not have time to regrow. In the years since, she had been hopeful that nature could fight back as she watched surviving corals take up symbionts that were more heat resistant. This year’s warming and the pace of bleaching already under way have dispelled that hope. What happens next is in some ways predictable. El Niño is not a haphazard force of destruction; it’s a warming phase in a specific area in the Pacific Ocean that scientists have determined shifts the probabilities for certain weather outcomes in various parts of the world. Those probabilities are reliable enough that, for example, the U.S. Navy already plans to send a hospital ship to the coast of Peru in February to be in position to help after expected floods. But as Baum and other scientists who study and love the delicate ecosystems in the equatorial Pacific are finding, just because El Niño is a familiar cycle doesn’t mean things will be the same when this one is over.

items.title: APM Terminals Apapa records 6% export growth in H1 of 2026
items.description: By Godwin Oritse APM Terminals Apapa, Nigeria’s largest container terminal, recorded a 6 per cent increase in export volumes in the first half of 2026, re-enforcing its continued efforts to boost the country’s non-oil exports and enhance Nigerian businesses’ access to international markets. Terminal Managing Director of APM Terminals Apapa, Kamal Alhraishat, attributed the growth to the resilience of Nigerian exporters, supported by a series of operational and service improvements designed to facilitate export trade. “Over the last five years, exports through our terminal have maintained a positive growth trajectory. This reflects both the resilience of Nigerian exporters and the targeted improvements we have made to facilitate export trade, simplify cargo flows and improve access to international markets,” Alhraishat said. He highlighted several initiatives introduced by the terminal to encourage exports, including dedicated export lanes at the terminal gate to accelerate cargo terminal access. “Our role goes beyond handling containers. We want to make it easier, faster and more competitive for Nigerian exporters to access global markets. Dedicated export lanes and our rail connectivity are all designed around that objective. “The rail connection between Lagos and Moniya (Ibadan) operates three times a week, providing exporters with an efficient alternative to road transportation. By reducing reliance on trucks and exposure to interstate and Apapa traffic, we can improve the predictability of cargo movement and help exporters reach international markets more efficiently,” he added. The terminal also receives export cargo through the Ebute Metta rail corridor, which facilitates cargo movement from various parts of Lagos, helping exporters avoid traffic congestion and reduce transit times to the port. Alhraishat noted that beyond operational improvements, the terminal continues to create platforms that encourage collaboration among stakeholders across the export value chain. “Through our Exporters Forum, now in its third year, we are creating a platform where exporters, government agencies, shipping lines, logistics partners and other stakeholders can come together to address real challenges across the export value chain. “The objective is not only to discuss these challenges, but to translate the feedback into practical actions that make Nigerian exports more efficient and competitive. Our next session is scheduled to hold at the terminal on Wednesday, September 2,” he said. The terminal’s major export commodities include soybeans, cashew nuts, cocoa, hibiscus flowers and solid minerals. Speaking on the significance of the Exporters Forum, Head of Commercial, Kayode Olufemi-Daniel, said the initiative aligns with the Federal Government’s drive to build an export-led economy. “Time is a critical factor in export trade, particularly for agricultural products. Delays within the supply chain can affect the quality of goods and, in some cases, render them unsuitable for export by the time they reach their destination. That is why we continuously review our operational processes and engage all stakeholders to identify opportunities for improvement and reduce delays across the value chain,” Olufemi-Daniel said. He added that APM Terminals Apapa remains committed to working with customers, government agencies and other industry partners to strengthen Nigeria’s export ecosystem and enhance the competitiveness of Nigerian products in global markets. The post APM Terminals Apapa records 6% export growth in H1 of 2026 appeared first on Vanguard News .

Alvarez rejoins Atletico Madrid training as move to Barcelona fades
items.description: Julián Alvarez has returned to training with his Atletico Madrid teammates after recovering from an illness that kept him out of the squad for several days. The Argentina international resumed group training on Sunday following Atletico’s victory over Sevilla at the Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán. Alvarez had been absent from team training for two days because of illness before spending another two sessions working individually as he followed a personalised recovery programme. His return comes with just two days remaining before the summer transfer window closes, with uncertainty continuing over his future at the Spanish club. Alvarez had not trained with his teammates since Atletico’s LaLiga meeting with Villarreal at the Metropolitano. However, he returned to individual work on Friday before joining the rest of the squad for Sunday’s session. The forward’s return is also significant for Atletico as the club prepares for its next LaLiga fixture against Athletic Club at San Mamés. The Madrid side is keen to have Alvarez fully integrated into the squad as quickly as possible if he remains at the club beyond the transfer deadline. Atletico sporting director Mateu Alemany had already expressed his desire to see the forward return to the squad. “We hope he rejoins quickly and is available for the next LaLiga match.” Alvarez was among the players who trained with the group on Sunday, while those who started against Sevilla carried out recovery work. With the transfer window set to close in two days, attention remains focused on whether Alvarez will stay at Atletico or make a late move elsewhere. For now, his return to group training provides a boost for Diego Simeone’s side as preparations begin for the trip to San Mamés. items.title: Afrique du Sud : la banque des BRICS accorde 405 millions de dollars pour des projets d’infrastructure
items.description: L'Afrique du Sud a signe deux accords de pret d'un montant cumule de 405 millions de dollars avec la New Development Bank (NDB), a annonce le 28 août le Tresor sud-africain. Un premier pret, de 200 millions de dollars, financera la construction d'un hopital tertiaire de 488 lits dans la province du Limpopo. Ce projet doit permettre d'ameliorer l'acces aux services de sante specialises dans cette region. Un second financement, de 205 millions de dollars, sera consacre au « Magalies Bulk Water Supply Scheme », un projet destine a repondre aux penuries d'eau qui touchent six municipalites des provinces du Limpopo et du Nord-Ouest. Dans ces zones, la demande en eau depasse actuellement les capacites d'approvisionnement disponibles. Les deux prets seront remboursables sur une periode de dix ans, avec une periode de grâce de quatre ans. Ils portent interet au taux quotidien SOFR, auquel s'ajoute une marge de 0,93508 point de pourcentage. Creee en 2015 par le Bresil, la Russie, l'Inde , la Chine et l'Afrique du Sud, la New Development Bank a pour objectif de financer des projets d'infrastructure et de developpement durable dans les economies emergentes. La banque s'est ensuite elargie a des pays non fondateurs a partir de 2021.

items.title: Nepal y Tíbet se enfrentan a una carrera contrarreloj en busca de más de 3.000 desaparecidos
items.description: En el quinto día desde que una gigantesca riada arrasase varios valles del Himalaya, dejando escenas desoladoras en Nepal y en Tíbet, la situación sigue siendo extremadamente complicada a ambos lados de la frontera . Las autoridades mantienen una carrera contrarreloj para salvar el mayor número de vidas. La catástrofe suma este domingo al menos 768 víctimas mortales (752 en suelo nepalí y 16 en la región autónoma china), mientras que más de 3.000 personas continúan en paradero desconocido. Entre los desaparecidos figuran todavía dos ciudadanos españoles, uno en Nepal y otro en Tíbet . Seguir leyendo

items.title: Nigerian-British boxer Moses Itauma discharged from hospital after losing to Hrgovic
items.description: British-Nigerian heavyweight boxer Moses Itauma has been discharged from hospital and is recovering at home with his family after suffering the first defeat of his professional boxing career. The 21-year-old was taken to hospital following his ninth-round stoppage loss to Croatia’s Filip Hrgovic in their fight for the vacant IBF heavyweight title at The O2 in London. Moses Itauma was carried out of the ring on a stretcher after appearing severely exhausted during the closing stages of the contest. His promoter, Frank Warren’s Queensberry Promotions, later confirmed that the young heavyweight had been given medical attention and was subsequently allowed to return home. “Moses is well. “He left the hospital last night and, after being checked over, he is now back home with his family,” Queensberry said in a statement. Itauma appeared to be in control for much of the fight and was reportedly ahead on the judges’ scorecards before Hrgovic turned the contest around in the later rounds. The British-Nigerian began to show signs of severe fatigue in the eighth round, leaving him vulnerable as Hrgovic increased the pressure. Referee Howard Foster eventually stopped the bout at 2:27 of the ninth round after Itauma was unable to adequately defend himself. Warren revealed after the fight that there had initially been concerns over a possible leg injury. “Moses has gone to hospital,” Warren said. “He has done something to his leg. He did something to his leg and he was exhausted, is the truth of it. It was a very fast-paced fight.” The promoter also acknowledged that Itauma would need to learn from the experience as he rebuilds his career. “He got caught and the fighting instinct was to stand there and let his shots go,” Warren said. “That’s what it is at the top level. You have to tick all the boxes. “He has got to learn from the fight and will hopefully do that.” Hrgovic, meanwhile, admitted that he had struggled against Itauma for much of the bout before finding the energy to change the outcome. “I was getting outboxed, but somehow I found the energy and the punch to change it all,” the Croatian said. He also praised Itauma, describing him as an exceptional fighter despite his lack of experience at the highest level. “He is the best fighter I have been in with but he needs more experience, he gassed out. I knew I had the pace in my favour. He gassed out but he is one of a kind.” The defeat ended Itauma’s unbeaten professional record but is unlikely to derail the highly rated heavyweight’s career, with his promoter already indicating that the young fighter will have an opportunity to learn and rebuild following the setback. items.title: Iran's supreme leader urges Gulf rulers in written message to unite against, confront 'real enemy'
items.description: Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei urged Muslim countries, particularly those in the Gulf, to unite against what he called their “real enemy” and said divisions among Muslims served the interests of their adversaries. The message was published on Mojtaba’s Telegram account for Islamic Unity Week, which marks the birth anniversary of the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH). It called for Muslim unity, cooperation in various fields and mutual defence, saying anyone who creates divisions among Muslims, “knowingly or unknowingly,” helps Islam’s enemies. “And how, in these times, can anyone attribute such an act to ignorance or negligence, when the tyrants of the world, led by the criminal US, have now cast aside the deceptive and flimsy masks concealing their ugly colonial aims and their hegemonic and domination-seeking schemes, removed their deceptive velvet gloves, and revealed their bloodstained claws to the entire world?” the supreme leader said, according to Iran’s Press TV . He asked whether Palestinians would have been left “so helpless” and “subjected to the oppression and crimes of the occupiers” if Muslims had been united. Mojtaba has not been seen in public since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, in which his father, the previous supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Mojtaba, was assassinated. His call for unity echoes a statement he made on Friday to Iranians, when he said he had banned actions that harm social cohesion and urged authorities to avoid “discouraging statements” that weaken national and public morale. Mojtaba specifically asked Gulf Arab rulers whether “rogues without identity” would have dared to covet their lands and possessions if the peoples and governments of the Gulf had been “united under the flag of Islam.” “My emphatic and repeated recommendation to the rulers of Islamic countries, especially the countries of West Asia and the Gulf, is to identify your real enemy, understand his plan and confront it,” Mojtaba said. Mojtaba, according to Iranian media, said that “unity among Muslims is the fundamental cornerstone for achieving a proud and dominant Islamic civilisation”. “This conceptual and intellectual framework, which embodies our aspirations for the Muslim world, has itself been realised to a considerable extent in our beloved Iran.”

items.title: 3 brothers killed, relative injured in IED blast in Balochistan's Duki: police
items.description: QUETTA: Three brothers were killed and one of their relatives was injured in a blast caused by an improvised explosive device (IED) in the Duki district of Balochistan on Sunday, police said. Duki Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Mansoor Ahmed Buzdar said the blast occurred while a pick-up truck was crossing a seasonal stream near the Killi Bakhtair Khan area of Luni tehsil. “Three brothers and one of their relatives were travelling in a pick-up on their way to their agricultural land in the area when they met the fatal incident,” SSP Buzdar said, adding three brothers were killed on the spot while their relative was injured in the blast. He said the blast was caused by a remote-controlled IED planted by unidentified miscreants. Soon after the blast, police and security personnel reached the site and shifted the bodies and injured to the district headquarters hospital, he said, adding that the pick-up truck was destroyed in the incident. Police said an investigation into the incident was underway. The incident took place against the backdrop of near-constant terrorist activity and lawlessness in Balochistan. On August 27, four terrorists belonging to Fitna-al-Hindustan — the term the state has designated for Balochistan-based groups to highlight India’s role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan — were killed in the Sasool area of Balochistan’s Khuzdar district, the military said. Days earlier, on August 22, a security official embraced martyrdom and six others sustained injuries in a roadside bomb explosion in the Khad Kocha area of the province’s Mastung district. Two days before that, four labourers were killed and three others injured in a blast in Mastung. The incident occurred in the Garo area of the Khud Kocha sub-tehsil — the same area where the provincial home minister Zia Ullah Langove survived an armed attack earlier this month, in which nine people, including six security guards, were injured. The Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies’ (PICSS) monthly security assessment said security situation deteriorated most significantly in Balochistan in the country last month. The overall death toll increased by 241 per cent in Balochistan, from 109 in June to 372 in July, the report said. Security personnel deaths in Balochistan increased from six in June to 62 in July, representing a rise of 933pc. Terrorist deaths rose from 75 to 238, while civilian deaths increased by 93pc, from 28 to 54. Eighteen members of peace committees were also killed in the province.

items.title: 5 top foldable phones cheaper than Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 7
items.description: Foldable phones have become some of the most expensive devices on the market, with Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 7 ranking high in the list. However, buyers do not necessarily have to spend a fortune to get a premium foldable phone. Several competitors offer book-style foldables with large inner displays, flagship processors and advanced cameras for less than Samsung’s latest Fold. Here are five options worth considering: 1. Motorola Razr Fold Motorola’s Razr Fold is one of the newest alternatives to Samsung’s foldable flagship and undercuts the Galaxy Z Fold 7 by about $100. The phone comes with a large 8.1-inch internal AMOLED display and a 6.6-inch external screen. It is powered by the Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 processor and comes with up to 16GB of RAM and a 6,000mAh battery. The device also supports 80W wired charging and features a triple 50MP rear camera system, including a 3x telephoto camera. For buyers who want a Samsung-style book-folding design but a lower starting price, the Razr Fold is one of the closest alternatives. 2. Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold Google’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold is another major competitor. The foldable features an 8-inch inner display and is built around Google’s software and Gemini AI features. Google also promotes it as its strongest Pixel device for multitasking and entertainment. The phone is particularly appealing to users who prioritise Google’s clean Android experience, AI features and camera capabilities while still wanting a large folding display. It offers a cheaper route into the premium book-style foldable category. 3. HONOR Magic V5 The HONOR Magic V5 is another strong rival to Samsung’s flagship foldable. It also offers twice the base storage of Samsung’s 256GB model at that price. The phone features a 7.95-inch internal OLED display, a 6.43-inch external display, Snapdragon 8 Elite processor, 16GB RAM and a 5,820mAh battery. Its slim design is another major attraction, while the camera system includes a 50MP main camera, 50MP ultrawide and 64MP telephoto camera. 4. OnePlus Open Although the OnePlus Open is an older model, its original starting price puts it well below the Galaxy Z Fold 7. The foldable comes with a Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 processor, 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage. It also packs a 4,805mAh battery with 67W fast charging. Its large foldable display makes it suitable for multitasking, while the generous storage and RAM remain attractive for users who want flagship-level hardware without paying Samsung’s latest Fold prices. Because it is an older model, however, buyers should check current availability and pricing before purchasing. 5. OPPO Find N5 OPPO’s Find N5 is another premium book-style foldable that costs less than the Galaxy Z Fold 7 in markets where it is sold. The phone launched in Singapore. One of its biggest selling points is its extremely slim design. OPPO says the Find N5 measures just 8.93mm when folded and 4.21mm when unfolded. It also comes with a Snapdragon 8 Elite processor, 16GB of RAM, 512GB of storage and a 5,600mAh battery. Vanguard News The post 5 top foldable phones cheaper than Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 7 appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Fix diapidated federal highways before Yuletide,Igbo group tasks Umahi
items.description: By Ugochukwu Alaribe UMUAHIA – The Igbo Community Association ,Abuja, has tasked the Minister of Works,Engr. David Umahi, to urgently make efforts to fix the federal highway linking the South East zone with other parts of the country before the yuletide. In a statement by its President General and Emmanuel Onah, Nze Ikenna Ellis- Ezenekwe and Emmanuel Onah, respectively, the group said it is worried over the silence of the federal government to the deplorable state of federal road networks connecting the South-East geo-political zone with the rest of the country. ​It noted that key arterial routes linking the South-East to the South-West, North-Central, and South-South regions have become death traps, causing motorists and commuters to suffer severe gridlock, destruction of vehicles, loss of lives and heightened security risks. The statement read;”​A striking case in point is the Benin-Agbor- Asaba corridor—a vital arterial gateway linking the South-West and South-East. “Despite initial public pushback and political friction when concerns were raised over this route, recent events and public outcry eventually led the Minister of Works, Engr. David Umahi, to inspect the corridor and offer an apology to stranded motorists for the severe hardship caused by the failed sections. “While we acknowledge the Minister’s recent intervention, this situation underscores a broader, systemic issue: critical transit routes leading into the South-East are routinely neglected until they reach catastrophic levels. “​As the Yuletide season approaches—a period characterized by high-volume travel across the country—it is imperative that the Federal Ministry of Works prioritizes immediate rehabilitation of these federal corridors. “Restoring these roads is essential not only to prevent avoidable road casualties but also to mitigate security vulnerabilities facing travelers. ​The Igbo Community Association also urged the federal government to ensure fairness and equity in the allocation of national infrastructure resources to the geo political zones. “South-Easterners are equal stakeholders in the Nigerian project and deserve safe, accessible, and functional federal road networks. ​”The ICA remains steadfast in its commitment to protecting the dignity of the Igbo-speaking people while advocating for infrastructure development that serves all Nigerians.” ​ The post Fix diapidated federal highways before Yuletide,Igbo group tasks Umahi appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 8 most expensive presidential jets in the world
items.description: Presidential and VIP jets are often fitted with luxurious cabins, private bedrooms, meeting rooms, advanced communications systems and other features designed to provide comfort, security and efficiency. Some governments also use modified commercial aircraft as official presidential transport, while wealthy individuals have spent hundreds of millions of dollars buying and customising aircraft to their preferences. Here are eight of the most expensive presidential and VIP jets associated with world leaders and wealthy individuals. 1. Air Force One – $660 million The United States presidential aircraft is among the most recognisable government jets in the world. The US presidential air transport fleet includes two specially configured Boeing 747-200B aircraft designated VC-25A. The term “Air Force One” is used as the call sign whenever the US president is aboard a US Air Force aircraft. The aircraft is equipped to serve as a flying command centre, allowing the president and senior officials to communicate securely while travelling. 2. Airbus A380 – $600 million An Airbus A380 reportedly commissioned for Saudi businessman and royal family member Prince Alwaleed bin Talal became one of the most talked-about private aircraft projects. The aircraft was reportedly valued at about $400 million before extensive customisation increased the overall cost. The A380’s enormous size offered the possibility of transforming the aircraft into a flying luxury residence, with space for lavish private and entertainment facilities. 3. Airbus A340-600 – $275 million An Airbus A340-600 associated with Jordan’s royal family is another aircraft frequently included among the world’s most expensive VIP jets. The wide-body aircraft stretches almost 76 metres and is powered by four Rolls-Royce Trent 500 engines. Its size and long-range capability make it suitable for intercontinental travel, while its VIP configuration provides a far more exclusive environment than a standard commercial aircraft. 4. Boeing 777-300ER – $260 million Bangladesh’s presidential aircraft is a Boeing 777-300ER, one of the world’s largest and longest-range commercial aircraft. The aircraft can undertake long-distance international journeys and has been configured for government travel. Its large cabin provides considerable space compared with conventional private jets, making it suitable for carrying government officials and other members of an official delegation. 5. Airbus A340-313 – $260 million Germany’s government has used specially configured Airbus aircraft for presidential and official government travel. The Airbus A340-313, named “Konrad Adenauer”, has served as part of Germany’s government transport fleet. Unlike conventional private jets, aircraft of this size can accommodate large government delegations while providing dedicated facilities for official business and long-distance diplomatic travel. 6. Boeing 747-430 – $220 million The Sultan of Brunei is associated with one of the world’s most lavish VIP Boeing 747 aircraft. The Boeing 747-430 is based on a commercial aircraft but has been extensively customised for private use. The aircraft is known for its luxurious interior, with the extensive modifications contributing substantially to its overall value. 7. Boeing 787 Dreamliner – $218 million The Boeing 787 Dreamliner has also been used for presidential transport. The aircraft associated with Tajikistan was originally delivered to Mexico before becoming part of the Central Asian country’s presidential fleet. The 787 is known for its fuel efficiency, long range and advanced cabin technology, making it well suited to long-distance government travel. 8. Airbus A340-500 – $200 million The Airbus A340-500 is another wide-body aircraft associated with VIP and government transportation. The aircraft is powered by four Rolls-Royce Trent 500 engines and is designed for long-distance travel. Its large cabin and long-range capabilities make it suitable for transporting senior government officials and delegations on international journeys. Vanguard News The post 8 most expensive presidential jets in the world appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Filière avicole au Burkina Faso : les vendeurs grossistes d’œufs s’organisent en faîtière pour mieux structurer le marché
items.description: Les vendeurs grossistes d’œufs du Burkina Faso disposent désormais d’une organisation faîtière. L’Union nationale des sociétés coopératives des vendeurs grossistes d’œufs du Burkina Faso a été officiellement mise en place ce 29 août 2026, avec l’installation d’un bureau de huit membres présidé par Salif Ouédraogo. L’initiative vise notamment à mieux organiser la commercialisation des œufs et à contribuer à réduire les ruptures sur le marché national. Dans les marchés et les points de vente, les œufs font partie des produits régulièrement recherchés par les ménages, les restaurants et les petits commerces. Derrière cette disponibilité apparente se trouve pourtant toute une chaîne, allant de l’élevage des volailles à la commercialisation. C’est sur ce dernier maillon que les vendeurs grossistes entendent désormais davantage s'organiser. « Seul, on va vite, mais ensemble, on va loin » , a expliqué Salif Ouédraogo pour justifier la création de l’Union. Selon lui, cette organisation doit permettre aux acteurs de mieux se connaître, de travailler dans la clarté et de défendre leurs intérêts tout en contribuant aux besoins des familles et du pays. Une organisation pour éviter les ruptures L’Union compte environ 100 membres, selon son président. Huit d’entre eux composent le bureau installé à l’issue de l’Assemblée générale constitutive. Pour Salif Ouédraogo, l’organisation des vendeurs grossistes doit également avoir des effets sur l’ensemble de la chaîne de valeur. Il estime qu’une meilleure commercialisation pourrait encourager les aviculteurs à accroître leur production et permettre ainsi de disposer de davantage d’œufs sur le marché. « Ceux qui élèvent les poulets pourront être encouragés à élever davantage afin que nous ayons davantage d’œufs à vendre, pour qu’il n’y ait plus de rupture d’œufs au Burkina Faso » , a-t-il déclaré. La question des prix constitue également l’un des enjeux mis en avant au cours de la rencontre. Le président de l’Union estime que la hausse des prix est notamment liée à l’insuffisance de l’offre. « Le manque qui crée l’élévation des prix » , a-t-il soutenu, en considérant que les difficultés de commercialisation ont, par le passé, pu limiter l’intérêt des producteurs à investir davantage dans la production. L’objectif du « zéro importation » La création de cette organisation est également perçue favorablement par Dasmané Traoré, défenseur des droits des consommateurs. Selon lui, les vendeurs grossistes occupent une place importante dans la distribution des œufs et leur meilleure organisation peut faciliter l’écoulement de la production avicole. « Les grossistes-vendeurs aujourd’hui sont incontournables dans la distribution des œufs au niveau du Burkina Faso » , a-t-il déclaré. Pour le défenseur des consommateurs, une meilleure circulation des œufs entre producteurs et commerçants peut contribuer à réduire les risques de mévente chez les aviculteurs et, à terme, favoriser une hausse de la production nationale. Il défend ainsi une ambition plus large qui est de réduire progressivement la dépendance aux importations d’œufs et tendre vers le « zéro importation ». « L’objectif final, c’est arriver de sorte à booster cette production pour qu’elle soit véritablement suffisante pour combler le vide qu’il y a aujourd’hui et tendre vers le zéro importation » , a-t-il expliqué. Dasmané Traoré estime par ailleurs que l’organisation collective donnera aux vendeurs grossistes un interlocuteur capable de porter leurs préoccupations auprès des autorités. Il a également évoqué les saisies récentes de produits importés et les interrogations liées, selon lui, à la qualité de certains de ces produits. Au-delà de la création d’une structure professionnelle, la nouvelle Union entend donc se positionner sur des questions qui concernent directement le consommateur à savoir, la disponibilité des œufs, leur prix et leur origine. Reste désormais à voir comment cette organisation traduira ses ambitions en actions concrètes auprès des producteurs et sur les marchés. Pour les ménages, l’enjeu sera surtout de voir si une meilleure structuration de la commercialisation peut effectivement contribuer à rendre les œufs plus disponibles et à limiter les fluctuations de leurs prix. Josué TIENDREBEOGO Faso7 L’article Filière avicole au Burkina Faso : les vendeurs grossistes d’œufs s’organisent en faîtière pour mieux structurer le marché est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Koulsé/Coopération : la Belgique prône « une diplomatie de l’action » au service des populations
items.description: BURKINA – BELGIQUE – COOPERATION – RESILIENCE – CHANGEMENTS – CLIMATIQUES Koulsé/Coopération : la Belgique prône « une diplomatie de l’action » au service des populations Korsimoro, 27 août 2026 (AIB) – Le vice-Premier ministre et ministre belge des Affaires étrangères, des Affaires européennes et de la Coopération au développement, Maxime Prévot, a réaffirmé, jeudi à Korsimoro, la volonté de la Belgique de poursuivre une coopération fondée sur des résultats concrets, à l’issue d’une visite de terrain consacrée à plusieurs projets soutenus au profit des populations de la région des Koulsé. Conduite par M. Prévot, la délégation belge, qui comprenait notamment l’ambassadeur de Belgique au Burkina Faso, Erwin De Wandel, et l’ambassadeur du Burkina Faso auprès du Royaume de Belgique, Léopold Bounkoungou, a visité plusieurs réalisations dans les domaines de l’agroécologie, de la santé et du relèvement au profit des populations de la région des Koulsé, notamment dans les communes de Korsimoro et de Kaya. Sous la conduite de la gouverneure par intérim de la région des Koulsé, Bernadette Adenyo/Sermé, et en présence de représentants des partenaires de mise en œuvre, la délégation a successivement visité une ferme agroécologique intégrée à Korsimoro, le centre médical du secteur 1 de Kaya, un site de personnes déplacées internes ainsi qu’un centre de formation. À l’issue de la visite de ces réalisations soutenues par la coopération belge dans le cadre d’un projet de renforcement de la résilience des ménages vulnérables face aux effets du changement climatique, le chef de la diplomatie belge s’est dit satisfait des résultats enregistrés sur le terrain. « On est au rendez-vous de la solidarité selon plusieurs axes », a résumé Maxime Prévot, assurant que les populations burkinabè peuvent « compter sur la coopération de la Belgique » pour poursuivre les efforts engagés. « Ce que je veux, c’est une coopération internationale de résultats, pas juste des grands discours. Il faut une diplomatie de l’action », a déclaré Maxime Prévot. Il a assuré que son pays poursuivra son accompagnement du Burkina Faso, en mettant l’accent sur les priorités définies par les autorités burkinabè. « Notre volonté, c’est d’être des partenaires qui appuient les priorités définies par les autorités burkinabè », a-t-il affirmé, insistant sur la nécessité d’assurer l’efficacité et le suivi des actions financées. Selon lui, la Belgique, partenaire du Burkina Faso depuis plusieurs décennies, prépare une nouvelle programmation de coopération. Une enveloppe d’environ 40 millions d’euros est déjà réservée à un programme de coopération spécifique avec le Burkina Faso, a-t-il indiqué, évoquant également 51 millions d’euros mobilisés en faveur de projets directs portés notamment par des ONG, en plus de l’assistance humanitaire. Pour la gouverneure par intérim des Koulsé, la ferme agroécologique intégrée de Korsimoro constitue un investissement structurant à fort impact pour les communautés locales. « Ce sont de grosses réalisations qui permettent à ces acteurs de pouvoir produire en toute saison. Ce sont des investissements structurants de ce genre que le gouvernement attend », a souligné Bernadette Adenyo/Sermé. Agence d’Information du Burkina ZO/aio/ata
